groups.sentence: Instructors define in their course policy what counts as AI, state its scope, and separate conventional tools like spell check from AI.
Instructors define generative AI as it applies to the course at the start of the course.
Generative AI means AI systems that create new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
The policy applies to all members of the university community, including students, faculty, staff and affiliates.
Artificial intelligence means computer systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence.
The policy covers academic work such as coursework, teaching, research, theses and assessments.
The policy names example tools it covers, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and DALL-E.
The policy covers AI features embedded in other software as well as standalone tools.
A tool counts as AI when it generates, rewrites, summarizes or substantively edits work, including help with brainstorming or outlining.
Sensitive, confidential and personally identifiable data and prompts or inputs to AI tools are defined.
Related terms such as hallucination, disclosure, AI literacy, human oversight and responsible AI are defined.
Agentic AI means AI systems that act autonomously, pursue goals across multiple steps and make decisions with little human intervention.
The policy does not apply to certain uses or groups, such as personal use, research, clinical or administrative work, or other schools.
All community members follow and comply with the policy.
Non-generative tools such as basic spell-checkers, calculators and search or sorting tools are not counted as generative AI.
Large language models are AI models that process and generate human language, and they are a subset of generative AI.
The policy covers all AI tools, including new ones released later, and focuses on uses rather than specific tools.
Administrators define generative and agentic AI and include AI-related terms in institutional definitions.
